rationale: Start with a broad, mid-length scouting gradient at moderate temperature to ensure all 10 compounds elute and to map the overall retention window and congestion pattern. The wide range and decent slope should avoid truncation while still giving useful selectivity information for later optimization.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only lever now is reducing analysis time. Shorten the gradient one step while keeping the same composition range and temperature to see how much t_last drops before any pair falls below 1.5.

We are very close to the ideal 10 min cutoff and the limiting pair is still above 1.5, so shorten the gradient one more step to try to bring the last peak under 10 min. Keeping phi0, phi1, and T fixed isolates the effect of slope on the critical pair.

At 14 min the 6/7 pair lost resolution, so recover selectivity with a small temperature increase while keeping the 16 min gradient that was already close to optimal. This tests whether higher T can shave a bit more retention without dropping the critical pair below 1.5.

The critical 6/7 pair is highly temperature-sensitive and likely late-gradient, so instead of changing T, raise phi0 one step to compress the early window while leaving the strong end unchanged. This may preserve or improve the 6/7 selectivity while pulling the whole chromatogram slightly earlier than the current 16 min method.

This is the obvious next step from the current best method: keep the improved phi0 that restored margin on the 6/7 pair, and shorten tG one step to try to get t_last under 10 min. If resolution holds, this should beat the current best.

The tradeoff is now very tight around the 6/7 pair, so keep the successful 16 min gradient and raise phi0 one more step to try to nudge the late region earlier without steepening the gradient. This tests whether further compression of the early segment can get t_last below 10 min while retaining enough resolution margin.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so now the only useful exploration is whether a faster method can preserve full resolution. Shortening tG one step from the current optimum directly tests the shortest possible fully resolved method around the best conditions.

The current best already achieves the maximum score, but a higher phi0 may still preserve full resolution while giving an even shorter method. Since tG 14 broke the 6/7 pair, keep tG at 16 and raise phi0 one more step to probe the fastest fully resolved boundary.

The optimum appears to sit on a narrow resolution boundary for the 6/7 pair, so test whether lowering phi1 slightly can restore or improve that pair while still keeping the last peak under 10 min. This explores end-strength selectivity rather than further compressing the start, which has already begun to hurt resolution.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical 6/7 resolution, so now test whether that extra margin allows a shorter 14 min gradient to retain full resolution while staying under 10 min. This is the most direct route to finding a faster fully resolved method than the current optimum.

Lowering phi1 increased the 6/7 resolution but slightly delayed the last peak; with the current best already at CRF 1.000, the remaining useful map is whether a bit lower phi1 at 16 min still stays under 10 min while adding more resolution margin. This will define whether injection 7 is sitting at the true optimum boundary or if a nearby equally optimal but more robust method exists.

We already have a maximum-CRF method, so the best remaining use of budget is to map robustness around it. A slightly shallower gradient at the same phi window and temperature should increase margin on the critical 6/7 pair and show how much robustness costs in run time relative to the current optimum.

Temperature had a strong negative effect at 45 C, so test one step lower than the optimum to see if cooler operation increases 6/7 selectivity enough to allow a more robust fully resolved method without pushing t_last past 10 min. This is the remaining nearby variable not yet mapped around the best point.

The temperature and phi1 effects are strongly nonuniform: higher T hurt 6/7 at phi1 0.95, while lower phi1 improved 6/7 at 40 C. Test their combination to see whether altered end-gradient composition can offset the temperature-driven selectivity loss and identify another fully resolved optimum region.

Both hotter and cooler temperatures changed selectivity dramatically, even shifting the critical pair, so a low-end temperature point will complete the local temperature map around the optimum. This checks whether the 40 C maximum is a true interior optimum or whether a more favorable low-temperature selectivity region exists.

With the local 25–45 C map showing strong, nonlinear temperature sensitivity, one high-temperature point will complete the trend and confirm whether selectivity deterioration continues monotonically above 45 C. This is still centered on the best composition and gradient, so it cleanly isolates temperature behavior around the optimum region.

Since 40 C is clearly the best temperature among those tested locally, the most informative remaining temperature check is the upper extreme to verify the direction and extent of high-temperature selectivity loss. This completes the practical temperature envelope around the established optimum without revisiting any prior grid point.

With the optimum already secured, the remaining useful search is a small composition map around it; combining the two individually promising changes, lower phi0 and lower phi1, will show whether their effects on the critical pair and t_last are additive or compensating. This helps define the shape of the local optimum basin around injection 7.

We have tested each side of the optimum separately; now combine higher phi0 with lower phi1 to see whether the faster elution from the stronger start can offset the longer retention from the weaker end while maintaining the improved 6/7 spacing. This fills in a key missing corner of the local composition map around the best method.

This new composition gives another CRF 1.000 point with the critical pair right at the threshold, so the next logical test is whether the same chemistry supports a shorter 14 min gradient. If resolution survives, it would identify a faster equally optimal operating point; if not, it confirms 16 min as the boundary here too.

The phi0 increase from 0.15 to 0.20 improved speed while only just preserving the critical pair at phi1 0.90, so one more step higher will define the upper phi0 limit for a fully resolved 16 min method in this promising region. This directly tests whether injection 20 is the edge or if an even stronger-start gradient can also achieve CRF 1.000.

At phi0 0.20 and phi1 0.90 we have a second CRF 1.000 point with only a slim 6/7 margin, so lowering phi1 one step may increase that margin while potentially still keeping t_last under 10 min thanks to the stronger start. This probes whether a more robust max-score method exists adjacent to injection 20.

The failure at phi0 0.25 with phi1 0.90 may have been driven by the narrower gradient window rather than phi0 alone, so widening the range back to phi1 0.95 tests whether 0.25 can still support a fully resolved 16 min method. This fills the last major gap in the local composition map around the max-score region.

For the final run, probe whether a slightly shallower gradient at phi0 0.20 and phi1 0.95 can recover full resolution margin while staying under 10 min, since the 16 min version was just short on the 6/7 pair but already comfortably fast. This is the last unexplored nearby condition with a realistic chance to join the max-score set.
